# Eye and orbit

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Ophthalmology > Basics of ophthalmology > Eye and orbit*

[Original Article Link](/library/cp0aoS)

---

## Summary

The eyes are paired, sensory organs that enable <u>vision</u>. Anatomically, the outer portion of the eye is divided into three layers: the fibrous tunic (<u>cornea</u> and <u>sclera</u>), the <u>vascular tunic</u> (<u>choroid</u>, <u>iris</u>, and <u>ciliary body</u>), and the <u>nervous tunic</u> (<u>retina</u>). The eye is further divided into an <u>anterior</u> segment, which contains the <u>lens</u> and structures <u>anterior</u> to it, and a <u>posterior</u> segment, which contains the <u>vitreous humor</u> and the <u>retina</u>. The <u>lens</u> is suspended between the <u>pupil</u> and the <u>vitreous body</u> by <u>ligaments</u> attached to the <u>ciliary body</u>. The <u>anterior</u> eye is subdivided further into two chambers: the <u>posterior</u> chamber (between <u>lens</u> and <u>iris</u>) and the <u>anterior</u> chamber (between <u>iris</u> and <u>cornea</u>), both of which are filled with <u>aqueous humor</u>. Functionally, the eye can be divided into structures that perceive light (components of the <u>visual pathway</u>) and structures that refract light (<u>refractive media</u>). The <u>visual pathway</u> begins with the first-order <u>neurons</u> of the <u>retina</u>, <u>retinal rods</u> and <u>cones</u>, which convert the optical image into neuronal signals, which are transmitted to the <u>brain</u>. The <u>refractive media</u>, comprising the <u>cornea</u>, <u>lens</u>, <u>aqueous humor</u>, and <u>vitreous body</u>, directs and refracts light to the <u>posterior</u> region of the <u>retina</u>. The eye receives its arterial supply from branches of the <u>ophthalmic artery</u> and drains into the <u>ophthalmic vein</u>. <u>Cranial nerves</u> mediate <u>vision</u> (<u>CN II</u>) and eye movement (<u>CN III</u>, IV, VI), while <u>accommodation</u> is mediated by fibers of the <u>autonomic nervous system</u>. The eyeball lies within the bony <u>orbit</u>, which has several openings for the passage of neurovascular structures. Accessory visual structures include the <u>lacrimal gland</u> and the <u>eyelid</u>. The <u>lacrimal gland</u> secretes tear fluid, which reduces friction and cleans the eye, while the <u>eyelid</u> protects the eyeball from excessive light, dryness, and foreign bodies. The development of the eye and accessory visual structures occurs between the 3<sup>rd</sup> and 10<sup>th</sup> week of <u>embryonic development</u>. <u>Extraocular muscles</u> connect the eyeball to the <u>orbit</u> and control movement of the <u>eyelid</u> as well as the eye.

---

## Gross anatomy

* Layers

* Fibrous tunic (external layer): <u>cornea</u> and <u>sclera</u>

* <u>Vascular tunic</u>/<u>uvea</u> (middle layer): <u>choroid</u>, <u>ciliary body</u>, pigmented <u>epithelium</u>, <u>iris</u>

* <u>Nervous tunic</u> (innermost layer): <u>retina</u>




* Segments

* <u>Anterior</u> segment:

* <u>Cornea</u>: refracts light

* <u>Iris</u>: regulates the amount of light impinging on the <u>retina</u>

* <u>Lens</u>: refracts light and focuses it on the <u>retina</u> by accommodating its convexity according to the distance of objects focused on

* Chambers

* <u>Anterior</u> chamber: between <u>cornea</u> and <u>iris</u>

* <u>Posterior</u> chamber: between <u>lens</u> and <u>iris</u>

* <u>Posterior</u> segment: 

* <u>Vitreous</u> chamber: between <u>lens</u> and <u>retina</u>, contains <u>vitreous humor</u>

* <u>Retina</u>: pigment cells translate light signals into neuronal signals that travel to the <u>brain</u> via the <u>optic nerve</u> (<u>CN II</u>)

* <u>Choroid</u>: supplies the <u>retina</u> with <u>nutrients</u>

* <u>Sclera</u>: protects the eye

* <u>Orbit</u>: bony structure that contains the eyeball and several openings for the passage of nerves, vessels, and <u>lymphatics</u>

* Vasculature: primarily derived from the <u>ophthalmic artery</u>

* Innervation: <u>Cranial nerves</u> mediate <u>vision</u> (<u>CN II</u>) and eye movement (<u>CN III</u>, IV, VI), <u>accommodation</u> is mediated by fibers of the <u>autonomic nervous system</u>.

* Accessory visual structures

* Eyelids: protect the eyes from excessive light, dryness, and foreign bodies

* <u>Lacrimal apparatus</u>: supplies tear fluid for the surface of the eyeball and the <u>eyelid</u>, minimizing friction and cleaning the eye (tear film)

* <u>Extraocular muscles</u>: control eye movement and elevation of the <u>eyelid</u>

## Layers of the eye

### Fibrous tunic (external layer)




The outer, fibrous coat of the eyeball is composed of the transparent <u>cornea</u> and the opaque <u>sclera</u>. Together, they form a protective capsule and maintain the eye's spherical shape. The <u>cornea</u> allows light to enter and is the major refractive surface of the eye, while the <u>sclera</u> provides attachment to the <u>extraocular muscles</u>.




| Important features of the fibrous tunic |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structures | Characteristics | Function |
| Cornea | <br><br>* <u>Anterior</u>, transparent part<br><br>* Avascular, provided with <u>nutrients</u> via <u>aqueous humor</u><br><br>* Expression of <u>insulin</u>-independent <u>GLUT1</u> transporters<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Refraction of light</u>, accounting for a greater part of the eye's optical power<br><br>* <u>Corneal reflex</u>: afferent arc of the <u>corneal reflex</u> is mediated by the <u>ophthalmic nerve</u> (<u>CN V<sub>1</sub></u>), the innervation of the <u>orbicularis oculi muscle</u> (efferent arc) is mediated by the <u>facial nerve</u> (<u>CN VII</u>)<br><br><br> |
| Sclera | <br><br>* <u>Posterior</u>, opaque, and fibrous part<br><br>* Contains the <u>optic nerve</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Protects the eye<br><br>* Maintains shape of the eyeball<br><br>* Provides attachments for <u>extraocular muscles</u><br><br><br> |
| Episclera | <br><br>* Outermost layer of the <u>sclera</u><br><br>* Contains vasculature<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Protects the eye<br><br>* Maintains shape of the eyeball<br><br><br> |





### <u>Vascular tunic</u> (middle layer): the <u>uvea</u>




The pigmented, <u>vascular tunic</u> of the eye consists of the <u>iris</u>, the <u>ciliary body</u>, and the <u>choroid</u>.




| Important features of the uvea |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structures | Characteristics | Function |
| Iris | <br><br>* A pigmented membrane with a central opening, the <u>pupil</u>, that adjusts its size in response to light<br><br>* Contains radial and circular <u>smooth muscle</u> fibers  <br><br>* Iris dilator muscle<br><br>* Radiating muscle fibers<br><br>* <u>Sympathetic</u> stimulation → dilation → <u>mydriasis</u><br><br>* Iris sphincter muscle<br><br>* Circular muscle fibers<br><br>* <u>Parasympathetic</u> stimulation → contraction→ <u>miosis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Regulates the amount of light that reaches the <u>retina</u><br><br>* Determines the color of the eye<br><br>* <u>Receptors</u><br><br>* α1 <u>adrenergic receptor</u> activation → dilation of <u>iris dilator muscle</u><br><br>* <u>M<sub>3</sub> receptor</u> activation → contraction of the <u>iris sphincter muscle</u><br><br><br> |
| Ciliary body | <br><br>* Located <u>posterior</u> to the <u>iris</u><br><br>* Composed of the ciliary ring, ciliary <u>epithelium</u> with ciliary processes, and <u>ciliary muscle</u><br><br>* Ciliary <u>epithelium</u><br><br>* Outer layer: pigmented<br><br>* Inner layer: not pigmented<br><br>* Ciliary processes: fibers that encircle the border of the <u>lens</u> and form suspensory <u>ligaments</u><br><br>* Ciliary muscle<br><br>* Composed of <u>smooth muscle cells</u><br><br>* Innervated by <u>parasympathetic</u> fibers derived from the <u>oculomotor nerve</u> (<u>CN III</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Accommodation</u>: adaptation of <u>lens</u> convexity and, accordingly, refractory power to maintain focus on objects at varying distances<br><br>* Produces <u>aqueous humor</u><br><br>* Anchors the <u>lens</u><br><br><br> |
| Choroid | <br>* Forms a dense network of pigmented stroma and <u>blood vessels</u><br><br> | <br>* Supplies the <u>retina</u> with <u>nutrients</u><br><br> |





![Muscles of the iris](media/tzj78bjb51r8qghnuotim2hj.jpg)

![Far and near point accommodation](media/dwia2dnnfeuk3u2vs66npbme.jpg)

### Innermost layer: the <u>retina</u> (<u>nervous tunic</u>)




On the gross anatomical level, the <u>retina</u>'s most important features are the <u>optic disc</u> and the <u>macula</u>. On a microanatomical level (see “Microscopic anatomy” below), it consists of neural cells that register light signals and translate them into neuronal signals that are transmitted to the <u>brain</u>.




| <br>Important features of the retina <br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structures | Characteristics | Function |
| Optic disc | <br><br>* Formed by <u>axons</u> of <u>ganglion</u> cells that leave the eye to form the <u>optic nerve</u><br><br>* Located medially to the <u>fovea centralis</u><br><br>* Insensitive to light due to lack of <u>photoreceptors</u> (physiologic <u>scotoma</u>, i.e, <u>blind spot</u>)<br><br>* Contains the optic cup<br><br>* Central, cup-like <u>depression</u> in the <u>optic disc</u><br><br>* Site of transversing of retinal vessels<br><br><br> | <br>* Point of exit for <u>ganglion</u> cell <u>axons</u> leaving the eye<br><br> |
| Macula | <br><br>* An oval-shaped yellow spot on the <u>lateral</u> side of the <u>optic disc</u>, near the center of the <u>posterior</u> wall of the <u>retina</u><br><br>* Lacks <u>blood vessels</u><br><br>* Contains the fovea centralis<br><br>* A central <u>depression</u> in the <u>macula</u> (foveola)<br><br>* Contains the highest density of <u>cones</u>, each of which is connected to a single <u>ganglion</u> cell<br><br><br> | <br>* Point of sharpest <u>vision</u> (100% <u>visual acuity</u>)<br><br> |

## Segments and chambers of the eye

### <u>Segments of the eye</u>




| Overview of the <u>segments of the eye</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Anterior</u> segment | <u>Posterior</u> segment |
| Divisions | <br>* <u>Anterior</u> and <u>posterior</u> chamber of the eye (filled with <u>aqueous humor</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Vitreous humor</u> within the <u>vitreous</u> chamber, <u>retina</u>, <u>choroid</u>, <u>sclera</u>, and terminal part of the <u>optic nerve</u><br><br> |
| Components | <br><br>* Lens: transparent, encapsulated, and flexible biconvex structure  <br><br>* Maintained in position by the suspensory <u>ligaments</u> of the <u>lens</u><br><br>* Attachments of the suspensory <u>ligaments</u>: ciliary processes (<u>lateral</u>), <u>lens</u> capsule (<u>medial</u>)<br><br>* Radially arranged fibers that connect the <u>lens</u> to the <u>ciliary body</u> (zonular fibers)<br><br>* Avascular, suspended in <u>aqueous humor</u> (provides nutrition)<br><br>* Function: <u>accommodation</u> (mediated by the <u>ciliary muscle</u>)<br><br>* Distant <u>vision</u> → decreased convexity<br><br>* Near <u>vision</u> → increased convexity<br><br>* Aqueous humor: watery fluid synthesized from blood plasma by the <u>ciliary body</u>, maintains <u>intraocular pressure</u> and provides <u>nutrients</u> to the <u>lens</u> and <u>cornea</u><br><br>* Other: <u>cornea</u>, <u>iris</u>, <u>ciliary body</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Vitreous humor<br><br>* Transparent gelatinous substance that fills the eyeball <u>posterior</u> to the <u>lens</u><br><br>* Provides support to the <u>lens</u> and holds the <u>retina</u> in place<br><br> |





![Intraocular lens](media/d4qwmarru5v4d6a30uetoqqm.jpg)

Intraocular lens




### Chambers of the eye




| Overview of the chambers of the eye |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Anterior</u> chamber | <u>Posterior</u> chamber | <u>Vitreous</u> chamber |
| Location | <br>* Between <u>cornea</u> and <u>iris</u><br><br> | <br>* Between <u>iris</u> and <u>lens</u><br><br> | <br>* Between <u>lens</u> and <u>retina</u><br><br> |
| Boundaries | <br><br>* <u>Anterior</u>: <u>posterior</u> surface of the <u>cornea</u><br><br>* <u>Posterior</u>: <u>anterior</u> surface of the <u>lens</u>, <u>iris</u>, and <u>ciliary body</u><br><br>* <u>Lateral</u>: <u>trabecular meshwork</u> and the <u>canal of Schlemm</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Anterior</u>: <u>posterior</u> surface of the <u>iris</u><br><br>* <u>Posterior</u>: <u>zonular fibers</u> of the <u>lens</u> and the <u>lens</u><br><br>* <u>Lateral</u>: ciliary processes<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Anterior</u>: <u>lens</u> and <u>retina</u><br><br>* <u>Posterior</u>: <u>retina</u><br><br>* Contains <u>vitreous humor</u> (occupies approx. 80% of the eyeball)<br><br><br> |





![Anterior chamber angle](media/j3ylj3b5tvj4s2hkm6ouli5i.jpg)

Anterior chamber angle




### Pathway of <u>aqueous humor</u> outflow




* Trabecular outflow (∼ 85%) [[1]](/library/2kXTMy)

* <u>Ciliary body</u> (nonpigmented <u>epithelium</u>) → <u>posterior</u> chamber → through the <u>pupil</u> → <u>anterior</u> chamber → trabecular meshwork with spaces of Fontana (in the iridocorneal angle) → canal of Schlemm → episcleral vessels

* Increased by muscarinic (<u>M<sub>3</sub></u>) <u>receptor</u> <u>agonists</u> (e.g., <u>pilocarpine</u> and <u>carbachol</u>)

* Uveoscleral outflow (∼ 15%)

* <u>Ciliary body</u> (nonpigmented <u>epithelium</u>) → <u>posterior</u> chamber → through the <u>pupil</u> → <u>anterior</u> chamber → direct drainage into <u>uvea</u> and <u>sclera</u>

* Increased by <u>prostaglandin</u> <u>agonists</u> (e.g., <u>latanoprost</u> and bimatoprost)

* <u>Aqueous humor</u> production is decreased by <u>carbonic anhydrase inhibitors</u> (e.g., <u>acetazolamide</u>), α2 <u>agonists</u> (e.g., <u>clonidine</u>, <u>brimonidine</u>), and <u>beta blockers</u> (e.g., <u>timolol</u>)

## Vasculature and innervation

### <u>Arteries</u>




The blood supply to the eye is primarily derived from the ophthalmic artery, a branch of the <u>internal carotid artery</u> that reaches the eye via the <u>optic canal</u>. The <u>arteries</u> listed below are all branches of the <u>ophthalmic artery</u>.




* Central artery of the retina

* Main branch of the <u>ophthalmic artery</u>

* Supplies the <u>retina</u> and parts of the <u>optic nerve</u>

* A <u>terminal artery</u> (no <u>anastomosis</u>)

* Travels in the <u>optic nerve</u>

* Divides into superior, inferior, nasal, and temporal branches

* Medial palpebral arteries: <u>anastomoses</u> with the <u>lateral</u> palpebral <u>arteries</u> to supply the <u>eyelid</u>

* Long posterior ciliary arteries: supply the <u>iris</u> and <u>ciliary body</u>

* Short posterior ciliary arteries: supply the <u>choroid</u>

* Muscular branches

* Supply the extraorbital muscles

* Branch into the anterior ciliary arteries that supply the <u>iris</u>

* Supraorbital artery

* Supplies part of the <u>orbit</u>, the forehead, and the scalp

* Passes through the <u>supraorbital foramen</u>

* Frontal artery: supplies the forehead and the scalp

* Lacrimal artery

* Supplies the <u>lacrimal gland</u>, <u>eyelid</u>, and <u>conjunctiva</u>

* Branches into the <u>lateral</u> palpebral <u>arteries</u>

* <u>Dorsal</u> nasal <u>artery</u>: supplies the <u>lacrimal sac</u>





![Arteries of eye and orbital cavity](media/qxhw5i4cwkoemfunwfzstdmv.jpg)

Arteries of eye and orbital cavity




### <u>Veins</u>




* Ophthalmic veins

* Superior <u>ophthalmic vein</u>: travels parallel to the <u>ophthalmic artery</u>

* Inferior <u>ophthalmic vein</u>: may divide into two branches

* One branch passes through the <u>inferior orbital fissure</u>

* The other branch passes through the <u>superior orbital fissure</u>

* Drain into the <u>cavernous sinus</u>

* Central vein of the retina

* Main pathway of retinal venous drainage

* Travels in the <u>optic nerve</u>

* Drains blood from the <u>capillaries</u> of the <u>retina</u>

* Drains into either superior <u>ophthalmic vein</u> or into the <u>cavernous sinus</u> directly

* Occlusion → restriction in blood supply (<u>ischemia</u>) and/or swelling (<u>edema</u>) → severe damage to the <u>retina</u> or blindness





> [!TIP]
> The <u>angular vein</u> forms an <u>anastomosis</u> from the <u>superficial</u> facial <u>veins</u> to the intracranial <u>veins</u>. Infections from the midface can spread via the <u>angular vein</u> to the <u>cavernous sinus</u> and sinus <u>veins</u>, potentially causing <u>cavernous sinus thrombosis</u> with life-threatening complications.




> [!TIP]
> <u>Cavernous sinus thrombosis</u> is one of the possible causes of <u>cavernous sinus syndrome</u>, which is characterized by a partial or complete loss of function of the <u>cranial nerves</u> passing through (i.e., <u>CN III</u>, <u>CN IV</u>, <u>CN V<sub>1</sub></u>, and <u>CN V<sub>2</sub></u>).




![Venous drainage of the orbit](media/k6f8l6putw55ux54p64pf5jf.jpg)

Venous drainage of the orbit




### Nerves




* <u>Ophthalmic nerve</u> (<u>CN V<sub>1</sub></u>)  

* Part of the <u>trigeminal nerve</u> arising from the <u>trigeminal</u> <u>ganglion</u>

* Supplies sensation to the forehead, <u>anterior</u> scalp, <u>lacrimal gland</u>, upper <u>eyelid</u>, and eyeball

* Receives <u>sympathetic</u> and <u>parasympathetic</u> nerve fibers that facilitate <u>pupil</u> dilation and innervate the <u>ciliary body</u>, <u>iris</u>, <u>lacrimal gland</u>, <u>conjunctiva</u>, and <u>cornea</u>

* Enters the <u>orbit</u> through the <u>superior orbital fissure</u> where it divides into its branches

* Branches of the <u>ophthalmic nerve</u>

* Lacrimal nerve

* Enters the <u>orbit</u> through the <u>superior orbital fissure</u>

* Innervates the <u>lacrimal gland</u>, the <u>skin</u> of the upper <u>eyelid</u>, and the <u>conjunctiva</u>

* Communicates with the zygomatic branch of the <u>maxillary nerve</u> (<u>CN V<sub>2</sub></u>), which may carry <u>postganglionic</u> <u>parasympathetic</u> fibers to the <u>lacrimal gland</u>

* Frontal nerve: enters the <u>orbit</u> through the <u>superior orbital fissure</u> and divides into

* Supratrochlear nerve: innervates the forehead, scalp, and upper <u>eyelid</u>

* Supraorbital nerve: innervates the <u>frontal sinus</u>, <u>conjunctiva</u>, scalp, forehead, and upper <u>eyelid</u>

* Nasociliary nerve

* Sensory limb (afferent limb) of the <u>corneal reflex</u>

* Enters the <u>orbit</u> through the <u>superior orbital fissure</u> and divides into

* Infratrochlear nerve

* <u>Posterior ethmoidal nerve</u>

* <u>Anterior ethmoidal nerve</u>

* Long ciliary nerves

* Supply <u>iris</u>, <u>ciliary body</u>, and <u>cornea</u>

* <u>Postganglionic</u> <u>sympathetic</u> fibers to the <u>iris dilator muscle</u> derived from the <u>superior cervical ganglion</u>

* <u>Sympathetic</u> fibers to facial <u>sweat glands</u> and smooth <u>eyelid</u> muscle

* Communicating branch to the <u>ciliary ganglion</u>





* <u>Optic nerve</u> (<u>CN II</u>)

* Leaves the <u>orbit</u> through the <u>optic canal</u>

* The crossing of the two <u>optic nerves</u>, one from each eye, forms the <u>optic chiasm</u>.

* <u>Maxillary nerve</u> (<u>CN V<sub>2</sub></u>)  

* Second branch of the <u>trigeminal nerve</u>

* Sensory innervation of the lower <u>eyelid</u>

* <u>Ciliary ganglion</u>

* <u>Parasympathetic</u> <u>ganglion</u>

* Located behind the eyeball, between the <u>lateral rectus muscle</u> and the <u>optic nerve</u>

* Short ciliary nerves arise from the <u>ciliary ganglion</u>

* <u>Postganglionic</u> <u>parasympathetic</u> fibers that innervate the <u>ciliary muscle</u> and the <u>iris sphincter muscle</u>

* <u>Sympathetic</u> <u>postganglionic</u> fibers (derived from the <u>superior cervical ganglion</u>) to the <u>iris dilator muscle</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Long ciliary nerves: long <u>pupil</u> diameter (<u>mydriasis</u>). Short ciliary nerves: short <u>pupil</u> diameter (<u>miosis</u>).

---

## Orbit

The <u>orbit</u> is a bony structure formed by the frontal, maxillary, <u>ethmoid</u>, <u>sphenoid</u>, lacrimal, and <u>zygomatic bones</u>. It contains the eyeball and openings for the passage of the <u>optic nerve</u> (<u>CN II</u>), vessels, and <u>lymphatics</u>.




### Walls of the <u>orbit</u>




* Superior (roof): lesser wing of the <u>sphenoid bone</u> and orbital portion of the <u>frontal bone</u>

* Inferior (floor): orbital surfaces of the <u>maxilla</u>, zygomatic, and <u>palatine bones</u>

* <u>Medial</u>: orbital plate of the <u>ethmoid bone</u>, body of the <u>sphenoid bone</u>, <u>frontal bone</u>, <u>lacrimal bone</u>, and the <u>maxilla</u>

* <u>Lateral</u>: greater wing of the <u>sphenoid</u>, orbital plate of the <u>frontal bone</u>, and the frontal process of the <u>zygomatic bone</u>





### Openings of the <u>orbit</u>




| Overview of openings of the <u>orbit</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Opening | Anatomy | Content |
| Superior orbital fissure | <br>* Between the greater and lesser wings of the <u>sphenoid</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Inside the common tendinous ring<br><br>* Nasociliary nerve (from <u>CN V<sub>1</sub></u>)<br><br>* <u>Oculomotor nerve</u> (<u>CN III</u>)<br><br>* <u>Abducens nerve</u> (<u>CN VI</u>)<br><br>* Outside the common tendinous ring<br><br>* Frontal nerve (from <u>CN V<sub>1</sub></u>)<br><br>* Lacrimalis nerve (from <u>CN V<sub>1</sub></u>)<br><br>* <u>Trochlear nerve</u> (<u>CN IV</u>)<br><br>* Superior <u>ophthalmic vein</u><br><br><br> |

## Eyelid

The <u>eyelid</u> protects the eyeball from excessive light, dryness, and foreign bodies. It receives sensory innervation from branches of the <u>trigeminal nerve</u> (<u>CN V</u>): the <u>ophthalmic nerve</u> (<u>CN V<sub>1</sub></u>) innervates the upper <u>eyelid</u>, while the lower <u>eyelid</u> receives sensory innervation from the <u>maxillary nerve</u> (<u>CN V<sub>2</sub></u>). The palpebral fissure (aperture) is formed by the upper and lower <u>eyelid</u>, which meet in the <u>lateral</u> and <u>medial</u> <u>canthi</u>. The following structures form the <u>eyelid</u>:




* <u>Skin</u> and <u>subcutaneous tissue</u>

* Thinnest <u>skin</u> of the body

* Very small amount of <u>fatty tissue</u>

* No <u>subcutaneous tissue</u> over the <u>lateral</u> and <u>medial</u> palpebral <u>ligaments</u>

* Orbicularis oculi muscle

* Innervated by the <u>facial nerve</u> (<u>CN VII</u>)

* Closes the eye

* Orbital septum

* <u>Connective tissue</u> that forms the <u>anterior</u> boundary of the <u>orbit</u>

* Runs from the margin of the eyelids to the <u>periosteum</u> of the orbital margin

* Within the <u>eyelid</u>, the <u>orbital septum</u> thickens and forms the <u>tarsal plates</u>, which provide stability to the <u>eyelid</u>.

* Landmark to differentiate between <u>preseptal cellulitis</u> and <u>orbital cellulitis</u>

* Tarsal plates

* Thickened extensions of the <u>orbital septum</u> composed of <u>dense connective tissue</u>

* Contain <u>tarsal glands</u>

* Superior <u>tarsal plate</u>: insertion site of the <u>superior tarsal muscle</u>

* Inferior <u>tarsal plate</u>: smaller, elliptical form

* Levator palpebrae superioris

* Originates from the roof of the <u>orbit</u> and inserts into the upper <u>eyelid</u> on the superior border of the <u>tarsal plate</u>

* Site of origin of the superior tarsal muscle (its primary function is to raise the <u>eyelid</u> and the <u>levator palpebrae superioris</u>)

* Innervated by the <u>oculomotor nerve</u> (<u>CN III</u>)

* Elevates the upper <u>eyelid</u> (opens the eye)

* Conjunctiva 

* Highly vascularized mucus membrane that lines the inside of the eyelids and the <u>sclera</u>

* Divided into two distinct layers

* Palpebral (tarsal) <u>conjunctiva</u>: lines the inner surface of the <u>eyelid</u>

* Bulbar <u>conjunctiva</u>: lines the <u>anterior</u> surface of the eyeball

* The palpebral <u>conjunctiva</u> transitions to bulbar <u>conjunctiva</u> in the superior and inferior fornices

* <u>Accessory glands</u> in the <u>conjunctiva</u> produce tear fluid (smaller volume than the <u>lacrimal apparatus</u>)

## Lacrimal system

### <u>Lacrimal apparatus</u>




The <u>lacrimal apparatus</u> supplies tear fluid to the surface of the eyeball and the <u>eyelid</u>, minimizing friction and cleaning the eye (tear film).




* Composition of tear fluid: consists of three layers

* Mucous layer (innermost layer)

* Mucins produced by <u>goblet cells</u> on the inside of the <u>conjunctiva</u>

* <u>Hydrophilic</u> layer that ensures stability and even distribution of the tear film

* Aqueous layer (middle layer)

* Isotonic fluid composed mainly of water, <u>electrolytes</u> (Na<sup>+</sup>, <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>, <u>Cl<sup>-</sup></u>, <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u>), <u>proteins</u> (<u>lysozyme</u>, <u>lactoferrin</u>, <u>defensins</u>), <u>EGF</u>, <u>IgA</u> secreted by the <u>lacrimal gland</u>

* Supplies the eye with <u>nutrients</u>

* Disposes of waste products

* Hydrates the <u>cornea</u> and lubricates the eye

* Lipid layer (outermost layer)

* Oils produced by <u>Meibomian glands</u>

* Prevents drying and cooling of the eye

* Lacrimal gland

* Located on the upper <u>lateral</u> part of the <u>orbit</u>, on the surface of the <u>levator palpebrae superioris</u> and the <u>lateral rectus muscle</u>

* <u>Serous gland</u> with tubuloalveolar secretory elements that secretes the watery fluid that makes up the aqueous layer of the tear fluid

* Drains via the 12 lacrimal ducts into the superior <u>conjunctival</u> fornix

* Innervated by <u>parasympathetic</u> fibers of the <u>facial nerve</u> (<u>CN VII</u>) via the <u>pterygopalatine ganglion</u>

* Tarsal glands (<u>Meibomian glands</u>)

* <u>Sebaceous glands</u>

* Located within the <u>tarsal plate</u> with orifices at the rim of the marginal zone of the <u>conjunctiva</u>

* Produce the oils that make the lipid layer of the tear film

* Lacrimal sac

* Dilated portion of the <u>nasolacrimal duct</u>

* Gathers tear fluid

* <u>Nasolacrimal duct</u>: drains into the <u>inferior meatus</u> of the nose

* Lacrimal punctum: an opening near the <u>medial</u> <u>eyelid</u> that collects tears produced by the associated <u>lacrimal gland</u>





![Lacrimal apparatus and tear film layers](media/gyk7keb74ek2khgufqnqrj3d.jpg)

Lacrimal apparatus and tear film layers




### Pathway of tears



* Produced in the <u>lacrimal gland</u> (below <u>lateral</u> eyebrow) → lacrimal ducts → superior <u>conjunctival</u> fornix → <u>anterior</u> eyeball → lacus lacrimalis → lacrimal canaliculi (at the inner <u>canthus</u>) → <u>lacrimal sac</u> → <u>nasolacrimal duct</u> → <u>inferior nasal meatus</u>

## Microscopic anatomy

### Layers of the <u>cornea</u>




The <u>cornea</u> consists of five layers (from <u>anterior</u> to <u>posterior</u>)




* Corneal <u>epithelium</u>: <u>stratified</u> squamous, nonkeratinizing <u>epithelium</u>

* Bowman membrane: <u>collagen fibrils</u>, no cells

* Substantia propria: <u>collagen fibers</u>, <u>fibroblasts</u>, <u>proteoglycans</u>, water

* Dua layer: thin, <u>collagen fibers</u>

* Descemet membrane: the <u>basement membrane</u> of the corneal <u>endothelium</u> (located between the stromal tissue of the <u>cornea</u> and the corneal <u>endothelium</u>)

* <u>Endothelium</u>: single layer of squamous cells





![Layers of the cornea](media/c8rbmoy653yp7ydblqky6ir1.jpg)

Layers of the cornea

![Layers of the cornea](media/cw6neoku8fupfk121588hotk.jpg)

Layers of the cornea




### Layers of the <u>iris</u>




The color of the <u>iris</u> (eye color) is determined primarily by <u>melanocyte</u> concentration in the <u>anterior</u> border and, to a lesser extent, in the <u>iris</u> stroma.




* <u>Anterior</u> border layer: network of <u>fibroblasts</u> with an underlying layer of <u>melanocytes</u> (modified layer of the <u>iris</u> stroma)

* <u>Iris</u> stroma: scattered <u>fibroblasts</u> and <u>melanocytes</u> in a collagenous matrix

* <u>Posterior</u> border layer: opaque pigmented <u>epithelium</u> (a continuation of the bilaminar ciliary <u>epithelium</u>)





![Microscopic anatomy of the iris](media/dfa8q8wgmhplye9ufu37caao.jpg)

Microscopic anatomy of the iris




### Layers of the <u>sclera</u>




The <u>sclera</u> consists of four layers (from outer to innermost)




* <u>Episclera</u>: thin layer of dense, fibrous tissue

* Stroma: <u>collagen fibers</u> that are orientated in different directions , <u>fibroblasts</u>, <u>elastic fibers</u>, <u>proteoglycans</u>

* Lamina fusca: pigmented cells and <u>collagen fibers</u>

* <u>Endothelium</u>: single layer of <u>endothelial</u> cells





### Layers of the retina (from <u>choroid</u> to <u>vitreous body</u>)




The <u>retina</u> consists of ten <u>retinal layers</u>. The outermost layer is the <u>retinal pigment epithelium</u>; the other nine layers (neural <u>retina</u>) consist of three types of neural cells: <u>photoreceptor</u> cells (<u>retinal rods</u> and <u>cones</u>), bipolar cells, and <u>ganglion</u> cells. These cells register light and translate this into neuronal signals that travel to the <u>brain</u> via the <u>optic nerve</u> (<u>CN II</u>).




* Bruch membrane

* The innermost layer of the <u>choroid</u>

* Lies adjacent to the <u>pigment epithelium</u> layer

* Site of <u>drusen</u> deposits in the dry (nonexudative) form of <u>age-related macular degeneration</u>.

* Pigment epithelium

* Outermost layer of the <u>retina</u>, adjacent to the <u>Bruch membrane</u>

* Contains <u>melanin</u> granules

* Aids in the formation of <u>rhodopsin</u> and storage of <u>vitamin A</u>

* Provides nutrition to <u>photoreceptors</u>

* Absorbs light and prevents reflection

* Separates easily from the neural <u>retina</u> in the event of trauma or disease due to a lack of junctional complexes connecting the two layers (<u>retinal detachment</u>).

* Not connected to the neural <u>retina</u> by junctional complexes → can easily be parted (<u>retinal detachment</u>)

* Layer of rods and <u>cones</u>

* Retinal rods: first-order <u>receptors</u> of slender, and cylindrical cells

* Primarily located around the <u>fovea centralis</u>

* Achromatic: <u>photoreceptors</u> specialized for night <u>vision</u> (dim light) and motion

* Contain rhodopsin: <u>visual pigment</u> and <u>G-protein</u>-coupled <u>receptor</u> that is activated by light (<u>phototransduction</u>)

* Retinal cones: first-order <u>receptors</u> of flask-shaped cells 

* Primarily located within the <u>fovea centralis</u>

* Chromatic (contain pigments for blue, red, and green light): <u>photoreceptors</u> specialized for <u>color vision</u>, bright light, and <u>visual acuity</u>

* Contain several types of visual pigments with different spectral <u>sensitivities</u> (enabling the distinction of colors)

* Rods and <u>cones</u> convert the optical image into neural activity, both using <u>glutamate</u> as a <u>neurotransmitter</u>

* External limiting membrane: supports <u>photoreceptor</u> cells

* <u>Outer nuclear membrane</u>: contains the <u>nuclei</u> of rods and <u>cones</u>

* External plexiform layer: contains <u>synapses</u> between bipolar and horizontal cells and <u>synapses</u> between the <u>photoreceptor</u> cells

* Inner nuclear layer

* Contains Müller cells (supporting <u>glial cells</u>), which extend from the inner limiting layer to the outer limiting layer

* Contains <u>the cell</u> bodies of bipolar <u>neurons</u> (second-order <u>neurons</u>) which transmit information from <u>cones</u> and rods to <u>ganglion</u> cells

* Internal plexiform layer: contains the <u>synapses</u> between ganglionic cells and bipolar <u>neurons</u>

* <u>Ganglion</u> cell layer: contain <u>neuroglia</u> and <u>nuclei</u> and cell bodies of <u>ganglion</u> cells

* Project to the <u>hypothalamus</u>, pretectal <u>nucleus</u>, <u>lateral geniculate body</u>, and <u>superior colliculus</u>

* Third-order <u>neurons</u> whose <u>axons</u> form the <u>optic nerve</u> (<u>CN II</u>)

* <u>Optic nerve</u> fibers: formed by <u>axons</u> of <u>ganglion</u> cells

* Internal limiting membrane: innermost layer; adjacent to the <u>vitreous humor</u>





> [!NOTE]
> The fovea Centralis contains mainly Cones, whereas the peripheral Retina contains mainly Rods.

## Function

* Eye (<u>vision</u>)

* Light reception and focus (<u>accommodation</u>): The eye dynamically adjusts to varying light levels, facilitating focus on both near and distant objects. 
* The size of the <u>pupil</u> primarily depends on the intensity of incoming light. For more details on <u>accommodation</u> and <u>pupillary</u> control, see: “<u>Accommodation (eye)</u>” in "<u>Visual processing</u>."

* Image processing: <u>retina</u> converts light into electrical signals

* Signal transmission: <u>optic nerve</u> (<u>CN II</u>) transmits these signals through the <u>visual pathway</u> to the <u>brain</u>'s <u>visual cortex</u> for interpretation

* Color and detail: <u>cones</u> are responsible for perceiving color and fine detail, while rods specialize in black-and-white <u>vision</u> and low-light conditions

* <u>Orbit</u>

* Protection from mechanical injuries

* Support and movement: provides attachment points for <u>extraocular muscles</u>, enabling smooth and coordinated eye movement (up, down, side-to-side, rotation)
* Eye motility is discussed in the section on “<u>Extraocular muscles</u>."

* Contains essential nerves, <u>blood vessels</u>, fat, and the <u>lacrimal apparatus</u>

* Related structures (eyelids and <u>lacrimal system</u>)

* Eyelids: protective barriers, distribute tears, and help maintain the eye's moisture through the blinking reflex

* <u>Lacrimal system</u>: production and drainage of tears, which lubricate and cleanse the eye's surface

## Extraocular muscles

The <u>orbit</u> contains 6 muscles that are attached to the eyeball. There is an additional muscle in the <u>orbit</u> that attaches to the upper <u>eyelid</u>, the <u>levator palpebrae superioris</u>, which is responsible for <u>eyelid</u> elevation.




| Overview of <u>extraocular muscles</u> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Muscle | <br>Function (Ocular movements) | Origin | Insertion | Innervation |
| Superior rectus muscle | <br>* Elevation, <u>adduction</u>, and intorsion (the inward, rotational movement of the eye) of the eyeball<br><br> | <br>* Common tendinous ring<br><br> | <br>* Upper globe<br><br> | <br>* <u>Oculomotor nerve</u> (<u>CN III</u>)<br><br> |
| Inferior rectus muscle | <br>* <u>Depression</u>, <u>extorsion</u>, and <u>adduction</u> of the eyeball<br><br> | <br>* Lower globe<br><br> |  |  |
| Medial rectus muscle | <br>* <u>Adduction</u> of the eyeball<br><br> | <br>* <u>Medial</u> globe<br><br> |  |  |
| Lateral rectus muscle | <br>* <u>Abduction</u> of the eyeball<br><br> | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> globe<br><br> | <br>* <u>Abducens nerve</u> (<u>CN VI</u>)<br><br> |  |
| Superior oblique muscle | <br>* <u>Intorsion</u>, <u>depression</u>, and <u>abduction</u> of the eyeball  [[2]](/library/r_Xfp00)<br><br> | <br><br>* Above the <u>optic canal</u>, on the body of <u>sphenoid bone</u> (and common tendinous ring)<br><br>* Travels through trochlea of <u>superior oblique</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Upper <u>posterior</u> globe<br><br> | <br>* <u>Trochlear nerve</u> (<u>CN IV</u>)<br><br> |
| Inferior oblique muscle | <br>* Elevation, <u>abduction</u>, and extorsion (the outward, rotational movement of the eye) of the eyeball<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> to the lacrimal groove<br><br>* On the floor of the <u>orbit</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Lower <u>posterior</u> globe<br><br> | <br>* <u>Oculomotor nerve</u> (<u>CN III</u>)<br><br> |

## Embryology

### Development of the eye




The development of the eye takes place between the 3<sup>rd</sup> and 10<sup>th</sup> week of <u>embryonic development</u>.




* Optic grooves arise from the neural fold bilaterally and develop into optic <u>vesicles</u> after closure of the <u>neural tube</u>.

* Optic <u>vesicles</u> induce changes in the <u>surface ectoderm</u> and begin to form the lens placode.

* The <u>lens placode</u> invaginates, giving rise to the <u>lens pit</u>.

* Simultaneously, optic <u>vesicles</u> begin to invaginate and form the <u>optic cup</u>.

* The <u>optic cup</u> has a central groove (choroidal fissure), which allows entrance of the <u>blood vessels</u> that supply the eye (hyaloid vessels).

* Failure to close the <u>choroidal fissure</u> by the 7<sup>th</sup> week of development results in coloboma, a unilateral or bilateral defect in a structure of the eye (e.g., <u>retina</u>, <u>optic disc</u>, <u>iris</u>) that typically manifests as a keyhole-shaped defect of the <u>iris</u>





![Embryological eye development: 3rd to 8th week of gestation](media/prrx7qx5y2bq2u2r0yivcarb.jpg)

Embryological eye development: 3rd to 8th week of gestation

![Coloboma of the iris](media/knkf30ijyrseqnqkbx9hxwji.jpg)

Coloboma of the iris




### Important structures and their derivatives




* <u>Neuroectoderm</u>: <u>retina</u>, <u>optic nerve</u>, <u>ciliary body</u>, <u>iris</u>

* <u>Surface ectoderm</u>: <u>lens</u>, <u>cornea</u> (<u>epithelium</u>), <u>lacrimal apparatus</u>, <u>skin</u> of the eyelids

* <u>Neural crest cells</u> or <u>mesoderm</u>: <u>cornea</u> (<u>endothelium</u>, <u>Descemet membrane</u>), <u>sclera</u>, <u>ciliary muscle</u>, <u>extraocular muscles</u>, <u>vitreous humor</u>





![Embryological eye development: 2nd to 9th month of gestation](media/wg83leyowxusygzv7eencln9.jpg)

Embryological eye development: 2nd to 9th month of gestation
